theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Kadian Lewis has just been made manager of a cost centre at a Kingston distribution firm, with an approved budget for the year. What should she do first?
options: Spend the first month's allowance quickly to set a pattern
Study each budget line, its assumptions and her spending limits
Ask finance to raise every line by the same small percentage
Wait for the first monthly report before looking at any figures

questions.stem: What does it mean to be the budget holder for a cost centre?
options: You prepare the whole firm's yearly accounts for the auditors
You approve the budgets of every other department
You answer for spending on that cost centre within its limits
You sign all cheques for the whole organisation

questions.stem: A supervisor may approve purchases up to J$150,000. She needs equipment costing J$210,000. What should she do?
options: Send it to the manager whose limit covers J$210,000
Split it into two orders of J$105,000 and sign both
Buy it on her own card and claim it back later
Approve it herself because it is in her budget line

questions.stem: Why do organisations set spending limits for each level of manager?
options: To make sure every purchase goes to the board
To slow down buying so that every budget ends up underspent
To let finance staff choose which suppliers to use
To match each decision to the right level of authority

questions.stem: A hotel department's yearly budget is phased by month. Why does the manager plan the timing of large purchases against this phasing?
options: So the monthly figures look smooth on every report
So that cash and budget are there when each cost falls
So the department can avoid getting any quotations
So that finance cannot see the purchases until year end

questions.stem: A stationery budget is J$240,000 for the year, phased evenly. After six months J$150,000 has been spent. What is the position to date?
options: J$30,000 over the budget to date
J$90,000 under the budget to date
J$30,000 under the budget to date
Exactly on budget for the period

questions.stem: Overtime for the quarter was budgeted at J$600,000. Actual overtime was J$690,000. What is the variance as a percentage of budget?
options: 13% adverse
9% adverse
15% favourable
15% adverse

questions.stem: A maintenance budget is J$1,200,000. J$700,000 has been spent and purchase orders worth J$350,000 are raised but not yet invoiced. How much is still free to commit?
Why should a manager track commitments (orders placed but not yet paid) as well as actual spending?
options: Because commitments are not part of the budget at all
Because suppliers refuse to deliver without this record
Because money already promised is not free to spend again
Because commitments are always cancelled before the year end

questions.stem: After nine months, a department has spent J$2,700,000 of its J$3,300,000 yearly budget. If spending continues at the same monthly rate, what will the full-year result be?
options: J$300,000 under budget
Exactly on budget
J$600,000 over budget
J$300,000 over budget

questions.stem: What is a reforecast during the budget year?
options: A fresh year-end estimate based on actual spending so far
A new budget that replaces the approved one without approval
A report of last year's spending used to start the next budget
A list of suppliers who have raised their prices this year

questions.stem: The fuel budget allowed 2,000 litres at J$200 a litre. The firm used exactly 2,000 litres, but paid J$230 a litre. What explains the variance?
options: A usage variance of J$30,000 adverse
A price variance of J$60,000 favourable
A price variance of J$60,000 adverse
A usage variance of J$60,000 adverse

questions.stem: A hotel allows J$150 of cleaning supplies per occupied room. The plan was 4,000 occupied rooms, but 4,600 were sold. Actual spend was J$680,000. How did housekeeping perform against the flexed budget?
options: J$80,000 over budget
J$10,000 over budget
J$80,000 under budget
J$10,000 under budget

questions.stem: A spending report shows a large underspend on repairs in March. The invoice for March's repairs has simply not arrived yet. What kind of variance is this?
options: A real saving that can now be spent on other budget lines
A timing difference that reverses once the invoice is posted
A price variance caused by the repair firm's new hourly rates
A sign that the repairs budget was set far too high

questions.stem: Damion Clarke manages a call centre in Montego Bay. Which variance is most within his control?
options: Rent set by a five-year lease signed by head office
Overtime caused by his own rostering decisions
The share of head office costs charged to his centre
A rise in electricity rates announced by the supplier

questions.stem: A finance report shows a J$45,000 overspend on cleaning in a department that bought no cleaning items that month. What should the manager check first?
options: Whether the cleaning budget should be doubled
Whether the cleaning staff have been stealing stock
Whether a cost was coded to the wrong budget line
Whether the report can be ignored until year end

questions.stem: A firm's policy is to investigate variances above 5% of a line or J$50,000, whichever is lower. Which variance must be investigated?
Overtime is running 20% over budget because two posts have been vacant for months. What is the best corrective action?
options: Fill or cover the vacant posts and review the rota
Ban all overtime at once whatever the service impact
Move the overtime cost to the training budget line
Accept the overspend and look again next year

questions.stem: A supplier raises the price of printing paper by 18% mid-year. Which response best protects the budget?
options: Stop all printing until the new financial year starts
Get new quotes and cut waste, such as needless printing
Pay the higher price and say nothing to anyone
Ask the supplier to invoice part of this year's cost next year

questions.stem: What is a virement?
options: An approved transfer of budget from one line to another
A payment to a supplier made by electronic bank transfer
A cut made to every budget line by the same amount
An extra grant added to the budget by a funding body

questions.stem: A school bursar wants to use savings on the security contract to pay for urgent roof repairs. What must she do?
options: Make the repair and code it to the security line
Leave both lines as they are and overspend on repairs
Ask the security firm to send the roofer's invoice
Get approval for the transfer under the school's rules

questions.stem: After a storm, a branch in Morant Bay needs urgent generator repairs costing J$380,000 that are not in the budget. What should the manager do?
options: Delay the repair until the next year's budget starts
Pay for it from petty cash in several small amounts
Report it, seek approval and record the reason clearly
Ask staff to share the cost from their own pockets

questions.stem: A department has a small contingency line. When should it be used?
options: For any item the manager would like to buy this year
For unforeseen costs, under the agreed approval rules
For paying bonuses to staff at the end of the year
For spending at year end so the money is not lost

questions.stem: In February, a manager has J$400,000 unspent and the year ends in March. Staff suggest buying items they do not need 'so we don't lose it'. What should the manager do?
options: Buy the items so next year's budget is not reduced
Pay suppliers in advance for next year's services
Spend it on a staff party to reward the team
Spend only on real needs and report the saving

questions.stem: A manager splits a J$600,000 purchase into four orders of J$150,000 so each falls within his own limit. What is wrong with this?
options: Nothing at all, if the total is within the yearly budget
It gets round the approval rules and is a control breach
Only that it creates more paperwork for the clerks
It is acceptable if the supplier gives a discount

questions.stem: A public agency's manager buys from the cheapest bidder, but the goods fail within a month. What principle was missed?
options: Value for money: price weighed with quality and life
Lowest price, which always gives the best result
Speed of delivery, which matters above all else
Supplier loyalty, which outweighs every other point

questions.stem: A manager in a ministry wants to award a cleaning contract to a firm without any quotes because it did good work before. What does the general aim of the public procurement rules require?
options: Use the same firm for as long as it gives good service
Award the work to whichever firm is based in the parish
A fair, open and recorded process that gets value for money
Let the permanent secretary's office pick the firm by phone

questions.stem: Why should a budget holder keep her own record of orders and spending as well as reading finance's monthly report?
options: So she can replace the finance system with her own
So she can check finance's report and spot errors early
So she does not need to talk to the finance office
So she can change the figures before the auditors visit

questions.stem: Sasha-Gaye Morgan's spending log shows J$1,020,000 for the quarter, but finance's report shows J$1,065,000. What should she do?
options: Accept finance's figure because it is the larger one
Accept her own figure because she placed the orders
Change her log to match finance and move on
Compare the items line by line and find the difference

questions.stem: Which monitoring routine is best for a department with a large and busy budget?
options: Look at the figures once, when the year has ended
Check only when finance sends an urgent warning
Review actual against budget each month, with reasons
Ask the auditors to tell the manager about problems

questions.stem: Which item is most useful in a monthly budget report to senior management?
options: Each variance above the threshold, its cause and the action
A full copy of every invoice received during the month
A list of all staff who used the photocopier that month
Only the total spend for the month, with no breakdown by line

questions.stem: A report uses red, amber and green to show each budget line. What does a red line usually signal?
options: The line is on track and needs no comment
The line has a minor variance within tolerance
The line is closed and cannot be spent again
The line is well off budget and needs action now

questions.stem: Kemar Ellis sees in July that his department will overspend by year end. When should he tell his director?
options: Now, with the forecast and his plan to correct it
At year end, when the final figures are known
Only if the director asks about the budget
After he has tried every fix without telling anyone

questions.stem: How can a manager best get her team to help control costs?
options: Keep the budget secret so staff do not worry
Share the targets and invite cost-saving ideas
Cut each person's supplies by half without notice
Tell staff that overspending will cost them their jobs

questions.stem: A team leader is given a small delegated budget for supplies. What should the manager give him with it?
options: Freedom to spend without any reporting at all
A personal bank card with no limit set
Clear limits, a simple log and regular check-ins
The whole department's budget to look after

questions.stem: Sales volumes at a Spanish Town bakery are 15% above plan. Ingredient spending is 12% above budget. How should the manager read this?
options: Ingredient costs are out of control and must be cut
The original budget for ingredients was set wrongly
Higher spending is linked to volume and is not alarming
Sales staff must be told to sell less next month

questions.stem: A department buys imported parts priced in US dollars. The J$ weakens against the US$ during the year. What will this do to its spending?
options: Lower the J$ cost of the same parts
Leave the J$ cost exactly the same
Raise the J$ cost of the same parts
Move the cost into the capital budget

questions.stem: A department is under budget, but the firm is short of cash this month. Finance asks managers to delay non-urgent buying. What should the manager do?
options: Ignore the request, since her budget is approved
Order everything early before any freeze begins
Ask suppliers to send their invoices to another department
Delay non-urgent items and keep essential services going

questions.stem: Which measure best shows whether a training unit is using its budget efficiently?
options: The total spent by the unit this year
The number of staff in the training unit
The number of courses listed in the brochure
The cost per trainee who completes a course

questions.stem: A health centre's training budget is 70% underspent at month nine because courses were postponed. What is the main risk?
options: Staff skills fall behind and planned goals are missed
The underspend will be taxed at the current GCT rate
Finance will close the department immediately
The underspend will cause an overdraft at the bank

questions.stem: Why should a manager record the reasons for each spending decision that departs from the plan?
options: So the decision can be explained and checked later
So nobody else needs to approve such decisions
So the department can avoid the next audit
So the record can replace the purchase order

questions.stem: At year end, a manager finds that utilities were overspent every month while stationery was always underspent. What should she do with this finding?
options: Nothing, since the year is over
Use it to set more realistic lines next year
Cut the stationery line to zero for next year
Ask finance to rewrite the year's figures

questions.stem: A firm's finance system lets budget holders see their spending online at any time. What is the main benefit?
options: Managers no longer need to approve any orders
Budget holders can change the ledger themselves
Problems can be spotted and acted on early
The monthly budget report can be dropped

questions.stem: A supplier offers Tamika Edwards, a budget holder, a free weekend at a hotel if she renews its contract. What should she do?
options: Accept it, as long as the contract price is fair
Accept it and share the weekend with her team
Ask the supplier to give the value as a discount instead
Decline it and report it under the firm's gifts policy

questions.stem: A manager must save J$500,000 in the last quarter without harming the service. Which approach is most sound?
options: Cut every line by the same percentage at once
Stop all spending on safety and maintenance
Rank spending by need and cut lowest-value items first
Delay paying all suppliers until the next financial year

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: A supplies line was budgeted at J$500,000 and actual spending was J$460,000. What is the size of the variance, in J$?
A yearly budget is J$800,000 and J$600,000 has been spent. What percentage of the budget has been spent?
J$360,000 of a budget is left and four months of the year remain. How much can be spent each month if it is spread evenly, in J$?
What is the one-word term for an approved transfer of money from one budget line to another?
What is the term for money promised through orders that have been placed but not yet invoiced or paid?
Spending was lower than budget. Is this variance favourable or adverse?
What is the expected final spending for the whole budget year, estimated part-way through it, usually called? (One word.)
What is a budget called that is adjusted to the actual level of activity, so that spending can be judged fairly? (One word plus 'budget'.)
A variance appears only because an invoice was posted a month later than planned. What two-word term describes it?
Which three-colour rating system, named by its colours' first letters, shows each budget line as on track, at risk or off track?
Overtime was budgeted at J$450,000 for the quarter and cost J$540,000. What is the variance as a percentage of budget?
What two-word term names the highest amount a manager is allowed to approve on her own signature?
What is the name of the small sum set aside within a budget to meet costs that could not be foreseen?
A budget allows J$80 of packaging per order. 5,500 orders were handled. What is the flexed packaging budget, in J$?
Which three-word phrase describes getting the best mix of cost, quality and useful life from spending?

essays.stem: You have just been given an approved yearly budget for your department. Describe the system you would set up to monitor and control spending against it through the year.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would study each budget line with finance so that I understand what it covers, how it is phased by month and the assumptions behind it. I would confirm my own spending limit and who approves above it. Next I would set up a simple spending log, kept with my administrative officer, that records every purchase order as a commitment when it is raised and as actual spending when the invoice is paid. Each month I would compare my log with the finance report, clear any coding errors and work out the variance on every line, to date and as a forecast to year end. Variances above the threshold in our policy would be investigated and explained, with an action and an owner. I would brief my team leaders on their parts of the budget and meet them monthly so that they share responsibility. Finally, I would send a short report to my director each month, using red, amber and green ratings, and raise any risk of overspending early, together with a plan to correct it.
markingPoints: Understands the lines, phasing, assumptions and spending limits first
Keeps a log of commitments and actual spending
Reconciles with finance each month and calculates variances to date and forecast
Investigates significant variances and sets actions with owners
Involves team leaders and reports regularly and early to senior management

essays.stem: A department's quarterly report shows: overtime budget J$450,000, actual J$540,000; supplies budget J$300,000, actual J$270,000; utilities budget J$250,000, actual J$262,500; training budget J$120,000, actual J$30,000. Calculate each variance and the total, and evaluate what the manager should conclude.
essays.modelAnswer: Overtime is J$90,000 adverse, which is 20% of its budget. Supplies are J$30,000 favourable, or 10%. Utilities are J$12,500 adverse, or 5%. Training is J$90,000 favourable, or 75%. The total budget is J$1,120,000 and actual spending is J$1,102,500, so the department is J$17,500 under budget overall. The total looks healthy, but it hides two serious problems. Overtime is well over budget, so the manager should find out why: vacant posts, sickness, poor rostering or more work than planned. Training is almost unspent, which is not a real saving if courses were postponed; staff skills may fall behind and the cost may simply move into the next quarter. The supplies saving should be checked to see whether it is real or a timing difference, such as a late invoice. The small utilities overspend may be due to a rate rise and needs watching rather than urgent action. The manager should act on overtime first, reschedule the training, and report all four lines, not just the total.
markingPoints: Correct line variances: overtime J$90,000 A (20%), supplies J$30,000 F (10%), utilities J$12,500 A (5%), training J$90,000 F (75%)
Correct total: J$1,120,000 budget, J$1,102,500 actual, J$17,500 favourable
Recognises that the total hides line problems
Explains likely causes and that the training underspend is a risk, not a saving
Recommends priorities: overtime action, reschedule training, check timing, report by line

essays.stem: By month seven your department is forecast to overspend its yearly budget by 8%. Plan the steps you would take to bring spending back within budget without harming essential services.
essays.modelAnswer: My first step would be to confirm the forecast by checking the figures with finance, clearing coding errors and separating timing differences from real overspending. Then I would find which lines are driving the overspend and why, for example overtime, a price rise or extra activity. I would tell my director early, with the facts and an outline plan, rather than wait for year end. Next I would rank our spending by how essential it is. Safety, legal duties and core services would be protected. I would look for savings in lower-value areas: delaying non-urgent purchases, getting fresh quotes, cutting waste, reviewing rotas to reduce overtime and pausing optional travel. Where a line is overspent for a good reason, such as higher demand, I would ask for a virement from an underspent line or a budget revision through the proper approval route. I would agree the actions with team leaders, set a target saving for each and track progress every month in a short report. Finally, I would record the causes so the next budget is set more realistically.
markingPoints: Checks the forecast and separates timing differences from real overspending
Identifies the lines and causes driving the overspend
Informs senior management early with a plan
Prioritises essential services and chooses targeted savings, not equal cuts
Uses proper approval routes (virement or revision), tracks progress and learns for next year

essays.stem: Explain why a manager should compare actual spending with a flexed budget, not only the original budget, when activity is different from the plan. Use an example from a hotel or a service firm.
essays.modelAnswer: An original budget is set for a planned level of activity. If activity changes, variable costs should change too, so a straight comparison can mislead. A flexed budget adjusts the variable cost allowances to the actual level of activity, while fixed costs stay as planned. For example, a call centre plans 50,000 calls and allows J$40 a call for call charges, a budget of J$2,000,000. It actually handles 42,000 calls and spends J$1,890,000. Against the original budget it appears J$110,000 under, and the manager might think costs are well controlled. The flexed budget is 42,000 times J$40, which is J$1,680,000, so the centre has really spent J$210,000 more than it should for that level of work. The opposite also happens: when activity rises, a team can look overspent when it has in fact been efficient. Using the flexed budget lets the manager separate the effect of volume from the effect of efficiency or price. This is fairer to staff, gives a truer picture to senior management and points the manager to the real problems, so that action is taken on the right lines.
markingPoints: Explains that variable costs should move with activity
Defines the flexed budget correctly (variable allowances flexed, fixed costs unchanged)
Uses a correct worked example
Explains that it separates volume effects from efficiency or price
Notes fairness to staff and truer reporting, including when activity falls

essays.stem: Evaluate the benefits and risks of delegating parts of a department's budget to team leaders, and recommend how a manager should do it.
essays.modelAnswer: Delegating parts of a budget brings decisions closer to the work. Team leaders know their needs best, so spending can be quicker and better targeted, and they become more aware of costs and more committed to the targets. It also develops them for more senior roles and frees the manager's time. The risks are that inexperienced team leaders may overspend, ignore the procurement rules, code costs wrongly or make decisions that suit their team but not the department. There is also a risk of weak records, which makes monitoring harder. I recommend that the manager delegate in stages. Each team leader should get a clear written allocation, a spending limit below the manager's own, and a short briefing on the rules for quotes, approvals and coding. A simple shared log should be kept and reviewed with the manager each month. Larger or unusual items should still come to the manager. As each team leader shows good control, their limit can be raised. The manager remains accountable for the whole budget, so she must keep checking.
markingPoints: Benefits: better-targeted decisions, cost awareness, development, manager's time
Risks: overspending, rule breaches, coding errors, narrow decisions, weak records
Recommends clear allocations and limits below the manager's own
Recommends training, a shared log and monthly review
Notes that the manager stays accountable and widens limits gradually

essays.stem: A hurricane damages your branch's roof and stock. The repairs and replacements are not in the budget. Describe how you would manage the finances of this situation.
essays.modelAnswer: Safety comes first, so I would secure the site and protect staff and remaining stock. Then I would record the damage with photographs, dates and a list of items, because these records will be needed for the insurance claim and for approvals. I would tell my director and finance at once, giving a first estimate of the cost and the effect on the budget. Urgent work to make the building safe would be approved under the emergency procedure in our rules, with the reasons written down. For the rest, I would get quotes as the procurement rules require and check what the insurance will cover, including the excess the firm must pay. I would ask finance whether the cost can be met from the contingency, a virement from other lines or a budget revision. I would keep all invoices and claim documents in one file and code the costs to a separate line so that they can be tracked. Finally, I would revise my forecast for the year and report the effect, and afterwards review what could be done better, such as storm preparation or insurance cover.
markingPoints: Makes the site safe and records the damage with evidence
Informs senior management and finance early with an estimate
Uses emergency and procurement procedures properly, with written reasons
Checks insurance cover and possible funding routes (contingency, virement, revision)
Tracks costs separately, revises the forecast and reviews lessons

essays.stem: Compare managing a budget in a government agency with managing a budget in a private firm. What extra care must a public-sector manager take?
essays.modelAnswer: In both settings a manager must keep spending within the approved budget, monitor variances and report honestly. A private firm, however, can often move money more freely between lines if it improves profit, and the owners or board decide how strict to be. In a government agency, the budget comes from public money approved through Parliament's process, so it must be spent only for the purposes approved. Transfers between lines need formal approval, and unspent money may have to be returned at year end rather than carried forward. Purchases must follow the procurement rules for public bodies, which require fair competition, proper records and value for money, so a manager cannot simply choose a familiar supplier. Public-sector spending is open to audit and to questions from the public and the media, so every decision needs a clear paper trail. A public manager must therefore plan purchases early to allow time for procurement, keep detailed records, avoid rushed year-end spending, declare any conflict of interest, and report variances through the proper channels. A private manager is still wise to do these things, but the public manager must.
markingPoints: Identifies common ground: control within budget, variance monitoring, honest reporting
Notes that public funds must be used for approved purposes and transfers need formal approval
Explains the procurement rules for public bodies in general terms (fair, recorded, value for money)
Notes audit, public accountability and year-end rules
Lists practical extra care: early planning, records, no rushed spending, conflicts declared

essays.stem: Explain how a manager can build a culture in which staff help to control costs, and justify why this matters.
essays.modelAnswer: Staff make many small spending decisions every day, such as how much stock to order, when to work overtime and how they use supplies and power. A manager alone cannot control all of these, so the team's attitude matters. To build a cost-aware culture, the manager should share the budget targets in simple terms and explain how spending links to the service and to jobs. Monthly figures for the team's main lines can be shown on a chart in the office. Staff should be invited to suggest savings, and good ideas should be tried quickly and the people who suggested them thanked in public. The manager should set a good example by following the approval rules and avoiding waste herself. Team leaders can be given small budgets of their own with clear limits. It is important not to blame staff for variances they cannot control, or they will hide problems. This approach matters because savings found by staff are often practical and lasting, people are more committed to targets they understand, and problems are reported earlier, which gives the manager time to act.
markingPoints: Explains that many spending decisions are made by staff
Shares targets and progress openly in simple terms
Invites and rewards cost-saving ideas
Leads by example and delegates small budgets with limits; avoids blame for uncontrollable items
Justifies: lasting savings, commitment and early reporting of problems

essays.stem: Describe the ethical risks a budget holder may face, and explain how she should deal with each one.
essays.modelAnswer: A budget holder controls money that belongs to the organisation, so she must act honestly and in its interest. One risk is pressure to get round the rules, for example by splitting an order to stay under her approval limit or by coding a cost to the wrong line to hide an overspend. She should refuse, follow the approval route and report the real position. A second risk is gifts or favours from suppliers, which can influence or seem to influence her choices. She should decline them and declare any offer under the gifts policy. A third risk is a conflict of interest, such as a relative bidding for work. She must declare it and stand aside from the decision. A fourth is year-end spending on things that are not needed, which wastes money. She should spend only on real needs and report savings. Finally, she may be tempted to keep bad news back. She should report variances honestly and early. Keeping clear records of every decision protects both her and the organisation.
markingPoints: Explains the duty to act honestly in the organisation's interest
Rule-breaking such as order splitting or miscoding, and the right response
Gifts and conflicts of interest: decline, declare, stand aside
Wasteful year-end spending and honest, early reporting
Keeps clear records of decisions

essays.stem: At the end of the budget year, how should a manager review her department's financial performance? Justify how the review should shape the next budget.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by comparing the final actual spending with the budget for each line and for the total, and by setting out the main variances and their causes. I would check which variances were controllable and which came from outside events, such as price rises or exchange rates. I would look at patterns across the months: lines that were overspent every month were probably set too low, while lines that were always underspent may have been padded or the activity did not happen. I would also look at what the money achieved, using measures such as cost per client served, not only whether we stayed within budget. I would ask team leaders for their view of what worked and what did not, including our monitoring routine and approval delays. The findings would go into a short report for my director. This review should shape the next budget because it gives evidence for realistic lines, shows where savings can be made, highlights risks to plan for, and improves how we monitor spending. Without it, the same mistakes are simply carried forward.
markingPoints: Compares final actual with budget by line and total, with causes
Separates controllable from uncontrollable variances
Looks for patterns and checks results achieved, not only spending
Involves team leaders and reports findings
Justifies use in setting realistic lines, savings, risks and better monitoring

practical1.title: Monitor a department's spending and prepare a variance report
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a data pack for one department of a made-up organisation (for example the maintenance department of a hotel in Negril, or the stores unit of a parish council): the approved yearly budget phased by month, a list of purchase orders raised, invoices paid for the first six months, and the finance office's monthly report, which contains two deliberate errors. As a group, set up a spending log in a spreadsheet, reconcile it with the finance report, calculate the variance on every line to date, forecast the year-end outturn, and write a one-page variance report to the director with red, amber and green ratings and an action for each significant variance. Give each member a named role: log keeper (enters commitments and actual spending), reconciler (compares the log with the finance report and finds the errors), variance analyst (works the variances and percentages, checked twice), forecaster (prepares the year-end outturn and the risk notes), and report writer (drafts the one-page report). In a group of four, the variance analyst also prepares the forecast. Photograph or screenshot each stage and hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Computers with spreadsheet software and a printer
photos: The flipchart plan showing roles and the steps the group agreed
The spending log on screen with commitments and actual spending
The reconciliation showing the two errors found and corrected
The variance table with amounts, percentages and RAG ratings
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Recorded commitments separately from actual spending
Found and explained the errors in the finance report
Variances and percentages are correct and were checked twice
Forecast outturn is worked correctly from the data given
Report explains causes and gives a realistic action and owner for each significant variance
Explained their part clearly when the assessor asked
safety: Use only the made-up data in the pack and keep the work confidential to the group and the assessor
Save work to the Centre's folder and do not share login details
Share the workload fairly and agree realistic times for each part
Take short screen breaks and keep cables out of walkways

practical2.title: Manage a mid-year overspend: role-played budget review meeting
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a scenario: a department of a made-up organisation (for example a call centre in Montego Bay or a ministry's regional office) is forecast to overspend its yearly budget by about 8% after a price rise, a storm repair and high overtime. As a group, prepare a corrective action plan that brings the forecast back within budget without harming essential services, then hold a 15-minute role-played budget review meeting with the 'director' (played by the assessor or a member of another group). Your plan must rank spending by priority, show each saving in J$ with its effect on service, state any virement or approval you need and the route for it, and set monthly checkpoints. Give each member a named role: chair of the meeting, finance lead (works the savings and the revised forecast, checked twice), operations lead (judges the effect on service and staff), procurement lead (checks quotes and approval rules for any new spending), and note-taker (keeps minutes and the action log). In a group of four, the chair also keeps the action log. Every member must speak in the meeting. Photograph each stage and hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Scenario and figures from the assessor
Computers with spreadsheet and word-processing software
Meeting agenda and action log templates
photos: The flipchart priority ranking of spending lines
The savings table and revised forecast on screen
The written corrective action plan with checkpoints
The minutes and action log from the meeting
checklist: Took a named role and spoke in the meeting
Savings are worked correctly and bring the forecast within budget, checked twice
Essential services and safety are protected, with reasons given for each cut
Any virement or extra approval follows the proper route
Monthly checkpoints and owners are set for each action
Spoke respectfully and answered the director's questions with facts
safety: Discuss staff costs in general terms only; never use real people's pay or names
Treat the role play respectfully; challenge ideas, not people
Keep the scenario and notes confidential to the group and the assessor
Keep the workload fair and take a short break between preparing and the meeting
